newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA makes new threat on ruling party official.
newsitem.headline: ETA makes new threat on ruling party official.

text.p: Basque separatist guerrillas have threatened to kill a second politician from Spain's ruling party just days after their assassination of a town councillor sparked massive protest demonstrations, an official said on Tuesday.
The new threat came in defiance of government vows to crush the rebel group ETA, which kidnapped 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco last week and shot him in the head on Saturday.

"It's true that a new threat against a member of the PP (Popular Party) has appeared," said Angel Acebes, general coordinator of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's party, told reporters on Tuesday. "We will reinforce all security measures," he added.

Blanco's killing was met with outrage across Spain. In an unprecedented condemnation, millions spilled out onto the streets for three straight days of protests against ETA and its political wing Herri Batasuna.

On Monday, when grieving family members were burying Blanco in his hometown of Ermua, grafitti appeared on the walls of a nearby Basque town of Renteria which said "You will be next", the daily El Pais reported.
The paper said the threat was directed at 63-year-old Jose Luis Caso, the only town councillor in Renteria.

Acebes confirmed newspaper reports that another Basque town councillor had received threats but he did not identify the official. He was speaking after a meeting of the party's executive committee with Aznar.
Earlier, Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja vowed to crush the rebels. "The government will do everything within its means to end terrorism," he declared.
He urged Spaniards not to fear a reaction from the violent separatists to the protests and the promised crackdown.
ETA's political arm Herri Batasuna said in a statement government attempts to isolate it could exacerbate the group's long-running conflict with the state.
Blanco's killing marked a turning point in the Spanish attitude toward the guerrillas. Basques who once whispered their opposition to ETA in private are now screaming it in public.
"This is a new phase which we must confront without fear," said Mayor Oreja, the government's top anti-terrorism policymaker.
Analysts said ETA's political influence was waning after the attack and the rebel group could answer the government's pledge to isolate them with more violence.
Spaniards have grown increasingly exasperated with ETA violence, which has accelerated since the beginning of the year.

The chilling kidnap and execution of a death threat against an ordinary person like Blanco -- an unpaid politician who played in a band and had plans to marry -- cut to the heart of Spanish society and caused a furore.
Millions of Spaniards filled the streets of Spain's two major cities, Madrid and Barcelona, on Monday night to vent their anger at the killing.

While most of the protests have been peaceful, the public backlash against ETA erupted in sporadic violence overnight in the Basque country, where Blanco was buried on Monday in his hometown of Ermua.
In San Sebastian, more than a thousand anti-ETA protesters hurled eggs and rocks at offices and a bar used by Herri Batasuna.
The people inside retaliated with Molotov cocktails, police said. At least two youths were injured and one person was arrested.
In Bilbao, Spanish media reported protestors attacked two ETA sympathisers in an assault on Herri Batasuna's headquarters. Similar clashes erupted in the Basque capital Vitoria.
ETA guerrillas abducted Blanco on Thursday and threatened to execute him in 48 hours unless 500 rebel inmates were moved to prisons in the autonomous Basque region.

Argentine Nobel peace laureate Adolfo Perez Esquivel, who has mediated between the guerrillas and the government in the past, said he had contacted an ETA leader directly last week to plead for the life of Blanco.
"He did not give any type of assurance about the situation," Esquivel was quoted as telling Spanish news agency Europa Press.
Blanco's killing was the 10th ETA assassination this year. The group has killed more than 800 people in a 29-year fight for an independent state.
